description: Hi! I'm Hamza, a student from Dubai passionate about space, physics, AI, robotics, engineering and game development. I enjoy coding, problem-solving and building interactive projects. For NASA Space Apps, I want to create a fun, educational astronaut-training game with space missions. I'm looking for teammates skilled in coding, 3D design, UI/UX or space science. Let's build something exciting!
summary:
ASTRA is a free 3D browser game for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. Players aged 9 to 14 run a crewed outpost on the Moon, then on Mars, and keep their crew alive by balancing power, air, water, food and radiation shielding.

Six short missions each teach one trade-off by making players live with it: solar power stops at night, making oxygen uses up water, grow lights compete with life support for stored power, and solar storms force a choice between sheltering and getting work done. Players build modules, drive rovers, make decisions where every option has a cost, and walk through their habitat in first person, where every console shows live mission numbers. Missions can be won or lost, and each debrief explains the real science. Solar storms are modelled on real events from NASA's DONKI database, and the Science library charts radiation measured at the Moon, on Mars and on the ISS (NASA OSDR RadLab).

Why it matters: the first crews on the Moon and Mars will face exactly these choices. ASTRA lets students practise this systems thinking, where every choice affects something else, free in any browser, including school Chromebooks and tablets.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

ASTRA is a free 3D browser game that puts students aged 9 to 14 in charge of a crewed outpost, first on the Moon and then on Mars. A campaign of six 10 to 20 minute missions (First Light, Ice Hunters, Green Thumb, Solar Storm, Red Planet, Mars Colony), plus Free Play, each builds around one idea that players learn by living with the consequences:

- Power: solar arrays only work in daylight; batteries carry the outpost through the night, and a forecast says when the battery will run out.

- Life support: each crew member needs 0.84 kg of oxygen, 3 L of water and 3 meals a day (NASA life support figures). On the Moon oxygen is made from water, so the rover mines ice in a crater that never sees the Sun; on Mars it is made from carbon dioxide, like NASA's MOXIE.

- Food: greenhouse grow lights compete with life support for stored power at night.

- Radiation: solar storms come with warnings; players choose a storm shelter, regolith shielding or both, and track each crew member's dose against a limit.

- Trade-offs: every module has a "catch", decision cards arrive mid-mission where every option costs something, and some choices come back later.

CAPCOM, a friendly voice at Mission Control, explains causes and warns before trouble. Every supply shows how long it will last, and time pauses for emergencies so players can think. Missions can be won or lost; each debrief shows a chart of what happened, the real science behind it, a NASA source and a quiz question.

Players can also step inside: a two-storey habitat with 14 rooms, furnished from real analogs (NASA's CHAPEA Mars Dune Alpha, HI-SEAS, the Mars Desert Research Station and the ISS), and a colony of 12 buildings around it. Its consoles show the simulation's live numbers, and some are the game's own controls: switch off the oxygen plant at its console and the HUD and the forecast change with it. Players can suit up, cycle the airlock and walk outside to repair modules, and drive two rovers: a crew rover that brings home ice and regolith, and a robotic science rover that maps buried ice with radar.

REAL NASA DATA

Every solar storm is modelled on a real solar particle event from NASA's DONKI database, and CAPCOM names it (for example the X5.8 flare of 11 May 2024). The Science library's "Real NASA data" tab charts the May 2024 storms as measured at the Moon (CRaTER on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter), on Mars (RAD on Curiosity) and on the ISS (DOSTEL), from NASA OSDR RadLab; cites six NASA OSDR studies behind crew health and the greenhouse; points to a real candidate Mars base site in NASA Mars Trek; and covers the Canadian Space Agency's food-production projects. A "Check the real Sun now" button asks DONKI for the last 30 days, live.

BENEFITS

- Students practise systems thinking: everything is connected, and a choice in one place shows up somewhere else later.

- Failing is safe and teaches: the debrief explains what happened and suggests what to try next.

- Teachers get a built-in page with learning goals, NGSS links and discussion questions, and can unlock any mission to teach one topic in a 10 to 20 minute lesson.

- It is free, needs no account or install, collects no personal data and works offline once loaded.

INTENDED IMPACT

Any classroom with a browser, including school Chromebooks and tablets, can use real NASA data to teach how a crew survives away from Earth: energy budgets, life support, food and radiation. We want students to leave understanding the trade-offs that real Moon and Mars crews will face, and wanting to learn more about space science and engineering.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React 19, Three.js (WebGL), Zustand, Vite and Vitest, hosted on GitHub Pages; sound is synthesised with the Web Audio API. Every 3D model, texture, sky and sound is generated by code while the game runs, with no downloaded models, images or sound files. 176 automated tests, including scripted wins and losses for every mission. Graphics adapt to the device so the game stays smooth on slower computers. No special hardware: it was built on a laptop and runs on laptops, Chromebooks and tablets.

Source code: https://github.com/HamzaAli0911/astra-mission-trainer

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

A live 3D outpost that students run from above and walk through on foot, with consoles that are real controls; real storms that CAPCOM names; and science shown honestly: there is no sound outside on the Moon, radiation and carbon dioxide are invisible (instruments show them, not coloured fog), and the sped-up clock always says how fast time is running.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age: one new idea per mission, plain language and rounded real numbers.

- Accuracy: numbers come from NASA and Canadian Space Agency sources cited in the game, and what we simplified is written down (docs/SCIENCE.md in the repository).

- Classrooms: short sessions, a teacher page, offline play and low-end school hardware.

- Accessibility: the Lexend typeface, high contrast, larger text, reduced motion, read-aloud, and keyboard and touch controls.

- Privacy: no accounts, no tracking and no personal data.

USE OF AI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)

We used Anthropic's Claude (Claude Code) as an AI coding assistant. It wrote most of the code, tests, documentation and in-game text from our ideas and instructions; we chose what to build, played and tested every version, and decided what to keep. The game's 3D visuals and sounds are made by that code while it runs; no AI image, video or audio generator models were used for the game. The 28-second demo video is real gameplay recorded from the game and edited with Claude, and its music and sound effects were synthesised by code written with Claude; it is marked "SI-generated video and audio" on screen and in its file metadata. Every commit in the repository carries a "Co-Authored-By: Claude" line.
